title: Alef-bet review
topic: review: reading with and without vowel marks
why: The big A0 review: the 22 letters, the final forms, the dagesh, the vowels, the geresh and reading with and without niqqud. We finish with a real self-introduction, so you start level A1 already able to read.

{"lessons": ["

The 22 letters at a glance

You now know the whole alef-bet. The most useful things to remember: the letters that sound the same, and the ones that change their sound with the dot (dagesh).

SoundLettersWatch out
silentא עonly carry the vowel
b / vבּ / בwith the dot: b; without: v
vב וtwo letters for v
kכּ קsame sound
khכ ך חsame raspy sound (like the ch in \"loch\")
p / fפּ / פ ףwith the dot: p; without: f
tת טsame sound
sס שׂsame sound; שׂ has the dot on the left
shשׁdot on the right
tsצ ץas in \"cats\"
hהsilent at the end of a word

The five final forms, always at the end of a word: ך ם ן ף ץ. And the three sounds from elsewhere, with the geresh: ג׳ (dj), ז׳ (j), צ׳ (tch).

", "

The vowels, with and without niqqud

SoundWith niqqudWithout niqqudExample
aמַ מָnothing, or ה / א at the end of a wordשַׁבָּת / שבת
eמֵ מֶnothing, or ה at the end of a wordקָפֶה / קפה
iמִoften יסִפּוּר / סיפור
oמֹ מוֹובֹּקֶר / בוקר
uמֻ מוּושֻׁלְחָן / שולחן
shva: nothing or a short eמְnothingמְאוֹד / מאוד

To read without vowels, keep your three reflexes: recognize frequent words at a glance (אני, זה, יש…), spot the prefixes ו ה ב ל מ ש, and think of the present-tense molds (לומד / לומדת).

The dagesh also disappears without niqqud: ב, כ and פ are read according to the word you know.

", "

You can read!

Here's a short self-introduction. Read it first with the vowels, then without: this is exactly what you'll see in Israel.

שָׁלוֹם! אֲנִי נֹעָה. אֲנִי סְטוּדֶנְטִית בְּתֵל אָבִיב, וַאֲנִי לוֹמֶדֶת מוּזִיקָה.Hello! I'm Noa. I'm a student in Tel Aviv, and I study music. [shalom! ani No'a. ani studentit be-Tel Aviv, va-ani lomedet muzika.]
שלום! אני נועה. אני סטודנטית בתל אביב, ואני לומדת מוזיקה.The same text, without vowels.

To ask where someone is from: מֵאֵיפֹה אַתָּה? to a man, מֵאֵיפֹה אַתְּ? to a woman. The answer is אֲנִי מִצָּרְפַת (I'm from France), with the prefix מ, \"from\"; just swap in your own country. To say where you live: אֲנִי גָּר (a man) or אֲנִי גָּרָה (a woman), followed by בְּ and the city.

In the next unit, you'll learn to introduce yourself in detail. The sentences will still have their vowels, but you now know how to read without them.
